|**2026-10-28**|**ObjectTwin: Measuring the Asset Correspondence Gap for Capture-Anchored Digital Twins**|Zhenghe Guo et.al.|Object-wise reconstruction increasingly inserts generated meshes into captured scenes as editable proxies for observed objects. This use creates a requirement absent from isolated-asset scores and pose estimates: at the captured metric state, the proxy should reproduce calibrated observations of the same instance. We present ObjectTwin, a scan-grounded measurement protocol that freezes the instance, cameras, scan-projected support and recorded depth, metric anchor, and evaluation denominator, then replaces only the object representation. The resulting asset correspondence gap measures lost observation agreement relative to scan-derived visible geometry without treating the scan as complete physical ground truth. Across two indoor RGB-D capture domains and two generation backends, visible, anchored generated assets lose 0.302-0.497 MaskIoU under this replacement. Every tested scene-level estimate is positive, while same-input generator preference reverses across capture domains. Coverage and overlap-depth analyses locate disagreement in both visible support and surface placement; the evaluated conservative pose refinement does not systematically recover it. These results establish capture correspondence as a separately measurable interface between generated-asset quality and stronger physical or task-level evaluation.|[2610.35904](http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35904)|
|**2026-10-28**|**Task-Utility IQA: Rethinking Image Quality Assessment in Embodied Tasks**|Jirong Zha et.al.|Image quality assessment (IQA) underpins embodied imaging pipelines by judging whether visual quality satisfies downstream tasks, yet most existing methods learn task-agnostic scores aligned with generic human ratings on static benchmarks. This objective mismatches embodied and interactive settings, where image adequacy depends on task goals, context, and action requirements that shape an agent's decisions. We argue that IQA should shift from score regression to goal-conditioned judgment defined by embodied task utility. To this end, we propose an MLLM-based embodied IQA agent framework that reasons about task requirements, grounds quality evidence, and produces decision-facing assessments. A compact VisDrone evidence study shows that conventional perceptual metrics and generic MLLM-based IQA scores are weak proxies for downstream VLM task success, while a task-conditioned utility score better predicts whether visual input supports the target task. These findings support a task-utility-oriented reframing of IQA for embodied, explainable, and decision-aware visual perception.|[2610.35905](http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35905)|
|**2026-10-28**|**Physiognomy Revisited: How Vision-Language Models Encode Sensitive Attributes Through Image Transformation**|Soumyajit Datta et.al.|Emergent generative AI technologies, while remarkably beneficial across several tasks and domains, can suffer from unforeseen vulnerabilities and difficult-to-anticipate failure modes. Such failure modes can disparately affect vulnerable communities. This paper investigates two well-known vision language models (VLMs) and inspects how these models encode protected identities while generating images. We show that when VLMs are requested to transform human face images to reflect race identities (e.g., Hispanic, Black, White, or Asian) and sexual orientation (e.g., gay or straight), VLMs often comply with such requests. We demonstrate that compliance (and refusal) is non-deterministic, group-sensitive, and generated images are statistically distinguishable, often accentuating deep-seated stereotypes. We further show that representation biases introduced during image generation can re-emerge in textual reasoning and characterization tasks. Finally, we show that this worrisome finding is not limited to racial identity or sexual orientation, image generation can perpetuate bias around criminality, raising concerning possibilities of AI-assisted profiling.|[2610.35910](http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35910)|
|**2026-10-28**|**Learning and Reasoning with Geometry: How Generation Helps Spatial Understanding**|Rui Yang et.al.|Image and video generators can produce spatially consistent visual content, but how to use this capability to improve spatial understanding remains underexplored. We study this problem from two perspectives: geometric supervision during training and explicit geometric evidence during inference. To this end, we introduce a unified geometric understanding and generation model (GeoUG) that integrates depth and multi-view generation with spatial understanding. First, we design a multi-scale depth codec that enables metric-depth generation using a pretrained visual autoencoder, and show that joint training yields task-dependent gains in spatial understanding. Second, we introduce 3DCueBench to control geometric difficulty while balancing selected 2D cues, and find that generated depth provides larger reasoning gains on questions requiring fine-grained geometric discrimination. Building on this finding, we develop adaptive interleaved reasoning, in which GeoUG first drafts an answer and then decides whether to generate geometric evidence to confirm or revise it. We train this decision through reinforcement learning, balancing accuracy gains over retaining the draft against generation cost. GeoUG achieves circular accuracies of 97.9%, 90.8%, and 94.2% on CV-Bench-3D, 3DCueBench, and DA-2K with fewer generation calls than always generating.|[2610.36022](http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36022)|
|**2026-10-28**|**Any3R: Feedforward 3D Reconstruction from Any Camera Type**|Jingong Chen et.al.|Geometry foundation models recover camera poses and dense geometry from a set of images with a feed-forward network, but they expect pinhole images. That assumption is inside the backbone too: the positional encoding and the training loss both bind an image position to a direction in space, and both depend on the lens. We condition both on the dense ray field, the unit direction through every pixel, which describes any central camera without a lens type, distortion coefficients or a bound on field of view. Angular coordinates give the rotary encoding the measured ray angle of each patch, evaluated per view, and solid-angle weighting scales the point loss by the area each pixel covers on the sphere, so neither the encoding nor the supervision depends on the lens. Any3R is therefore a feed-forward model that takes any central camera, and is robust to mixing many camera types per scene, with no retraining per lens. On a benchmark of thirteen central cameras across three datasets, where every method reconstructs with its own predicted camera poses, it is the most consistently accurate method. Any3R enables scalable 3D reconstruction from heterogeneous crowdsourced and archival imagery collections sourced across diverse camera types. Project page: https://jingong-chen.github.io/Any3R/|[2610.36150](http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36150)|
|**2026-10-28**|**PrinGS: Privacy Preservation in Gaussian Splatting**|Gaurav Behera et.al.|3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has rapidly become the preferred representation for high-fidelity novel view synthesis and 3D scene reconstruction. However, the learned representation encodes sensitive visual information including human faces, license plates, documents, and computer screens, raising significant privacy concerns when trained splats are shared or deployed. In this work, we address the underexplored problem of privacy preservation in Gaussian Splatting by proposing a representation-level anonymization framework that directly anonymizes a trained splat. Given a trained splat and a user-provided reference view identifying sensitive content, our method localizes the corresponding regions in the underlying 3D representation and directly anonymizes them, ensuring that the sensitive information is absent from all subsequently rendered novel views while preserving the overall scene geometry and visual fidelity. We achieve this post-training anonymization in less than 1 second. Furthermore, we extend our framework with a privacy-by-design training strategy that prevents sensitive content from being embedded into the representation during optimization, enabling the generation of privacy-preserving splats directly from training images. Our method achieves a remarkably low Face Similarity Measure (FSM) of 9.79% at a retained Face Detection Rate (FDR) of 39.47% and makes sensitive text completely unreadable with an OCR Character Error Rate of 1.00. Our work aims to serve as the primary stepping stone towards privacy-aware 3D representations and motivates further research along these directions.|[2610.36168](http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36168)|
|**2026-10-28**|**Beyond the Estimate: Wiener-Informed Decoding for Easier Training of Pixel-Space Flow Models**|Ziqiao Wang et.al.|Learning velocity fields directly in pixel space is difficult and slow. We show that coarse second-order image statistics can ease this task: frozen Wiener estimates improve velocity learning, with gains extending beyond the linear predictions they explicitly provide. Moreover, we observe similar but complementary gains from frozen bases and pixel decoding. These observations motivate Wiener-informed Decoding (WiD), which uses statistical knowledge both for direct prediction and to organize decoder computation without modifying native blocks. WiD combines a trainable Wiener prediction path with coefficient interfaces that inject features into the native decoder and return its predicted coefficient corrections, with these components initialized with data statistics. All introduced parameters, including the spectrum and coordinate transforms, are trained jointly under the original pixel-space velocity objective. Across model scales and decoder architectures, WiD accelerates training and improves generation quality with modest parameter overhead. It also yields smoother gradient trajectories and remains effective with representation alignment. WiD improves class-conditional and text-to-image generation across different resolutions. On ImageNet 256 x 256, PixelDiT-XL with WiD reaches FID 1.53 after 500 epochs, achieving comparable quality to PixelDiT with 37.5% fewer training epochs. Statistical denoisers contribute beyond the estimate: their computational structure can also ease pixel-space training.|[2610.36192](http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36192)|
|**2026-10-28**|**Learning to Read Braille: Benchmarking and Improving Braille Recognition Capabilities of VLMs**|Kartik Jangra et.al.|Despite rapid progress in visual understanding and document transcription, modern vision-language models (VLMs) struggle with a fundamental accessibility task: reading Braille from images. We introduce BrailleBench, a manually curated benchmark of 259 real-world Grade-1 and Grade-2 Braille images. We evaluate proprietary, open-weight, OCR-specialized, and tool-assisted multimodal systems and find that standalone general-purpose models perform poorly at directly transcribing Braille images, whereas tool-assisted systems perform much better. We design a synthetic Braille generation pipeline with diverse layouts and image perturbations. A 2B VLM model trained on our synthetic data reaches 87% exact match on Grade-1 and 61% on Grade-2 BrailleBench, outperforming standalone VLMs and achieving the highest Grade-2 exact match score among the evaluated systems. We further show that high accuracy on synthetic validation data does not guarantee high accuracy on real photographs in our experiments: models trained on prior synthetic data reach up to 96% on their synthetic validation set but at most 3.26% on Grade-1 BrailleBench. Our results identify an accessibility-relevant capability gap in multimodal systems and show that targeted synthetic supervision can improve real-world Braille transcription.|[2610.36195](http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36195)|
|**2026-10-28**|**UT-HMR: Uncertainty-Guided Temporal Modeling for Robust 3D Human Mesh Recovery**|Zhibo Wang et.al.|Monocular 3D human mesh recovery (HMR) remains unreliable under weak observations caused by long camera-to-person distances, occlusion, and motion blur. In challenging scenarios such as sports, these factors make the problem highly ambiguous, as different 3D poses may yield similar 2D projections. This ambiguity is especially severe for one-stage HMR, which recovers all meshes directly from the full image without person crops or external 2D cues. To handle this ambiguity, we present UT-HMR ( Uncertainty-guided Temporal HMR), to our knowledge the first one-stage HMR framework to capture correlated pose uncertainty across joints. Each person query predicts a Gaussian distribution over the full SMPL pose with a compact low-rank-plus-diagonal covariance, which is converted into joint-wise precision weights for heteroscedastic supervision while keeping inference deterministic. Temporal early fusion further injects neighboring-frame evidence before pose decoding, supplying the visual evidence needed to resolve the ambiguity that the uncertainty captures. With a lightweight ViT-B backbone, UT-HMR achieves state-of-the-art results on VIP-HockeyPose-v2 (ice hockey) and WorldPose (soccer), reducing MPJPE, PA-MPJPE, and PVE by up to 4.7%, 3.8%, and 5.6%, and remains competitive on 3DPW against methods with larger backbones and higher input resolutions.|[2610.36203](http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36203)|
|**2026-10-28**|**Diagnosing and Correcting Bias in MLLM for Long Video Understanding**|Xusheng Liang et.al.|Long-video question answering is challenging since the answer often hinges on a few decisive moments scattered throughout the video, while memory constraints force Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to sample frames at extremely low rates, resulting in sparsity that risks omitting key evidence. Though aggressively enlarging the context size is intuitive, we argue that performance remains fundamentally constrained by the bias, \emph{i.e.}, the misleading cues caused by spurious \textit{linguistic} correlations and salient yet irrelevant \textit{visual} observations. In this paper, we first introduce {S-MME}, a benchmark designed to systematically diagnose shortcut-biased behavior in MLLMs. To mitigate this failure, we further propose a training-free framework, Counterfactual Long-video Evidence-Aware Reasoning (CLEAR). By treating the full video-question pair as a complete view, CLEAR estimates bias effects via augmented views by only keeping the question or locally salient visual clips. Then, we intervene hidden states to mitigate the discrepancy at inference such that the correct answer can be predicted confidently. With experimental studies across five benchmarks, we show that our method is generalizable and can be integrated in different MLLMs, yielding consistent gains in prediction and robustness. We hope CLEAR can offer a complementary direction in test-time scaling for long-video understanding.|[2610.36210](http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36210)|
|**2026-10-28**|**Hierarchical Multimodal Interaction Reasoning for Dyadic Relationship Recognition**|Wang Tang et.al.|Dyadic relationship recognition aims to identify the latent social relationship between two individuals from their multimodal interactions. Existing methods typically project heterogeneous cues into a shared representation and optimise a flat classification objective, overlooking that relationships may rely on different interaction patterns. For instance, distant relationships can often be inferred from direct behavioural correspondence, whereas close relationships are better reflected by coordinated affective, behavioural, and multimodal responses. To address this limitation, we propose HiRe-DRR, a Hierarchical Multimodal Interaction Reasoning framework that organises relationship evidence from three complementary perspectives: feature level, interaction type, and relationship hierarchy. HiRe-DRR decomposes facial, bodily, acoustic, and textual cues into low- and high-level representations and constructs homogeneous and heterogeneous cross-participant interactions. We further introduce the Mixture-of-Interaction Transformer (MoI-Former), which treats diverse interactions as specialised experts and employs relation-aware sparse routing to identify relationship-relevant evidence while preserving contextual interaction information. The proposed Hierarchical Conditional Loss (HC-Loss) exploits the hierarchical nature of social relationships through coarse-to-fine supervision, enabling structured relationship reasoning. Extensive experiments on three dyadic relationship benchmarks demonstrate that HiRe-DRR outperforms recent representative image-, video-, and multimodal methods. Our routing analysis further reveals that distant relationships tend to rely on low-level homogeneous interactions, whereas closer relationships focus on high-level heterogeneous interactions. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/tw-repository/HiRe-DRR.|[2610.36249](http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36249)|
|**2026-10-28**|**Cross-modal Steering Vectors Exist Across Both Image and Text Generation**|Donghao Zeng (Mila et.al.|Are concepts and mechanisms unified across modalities in current AI models, or instead implemented separately for each one? We operationalize this broad question of modality unification by studying cross-modal steering: 1) finding vectors that successfully steer generation on tokens of one modality, which then 2) transfer zero-shot to steer generation when added to tokens of another modality. Our study goes beyond simple correlational alignment (e.g. representational similarity) because steering is fundamentally causal. We study cross-modal steering in several unified multimodal models (UMMs), since they possess shared parameters for language and image generation, focusing on these two modalities. Across diverse steered concepts such as emotion and object size, we show that steering vectors transfer zero-shot in both directions (text-to-image & image-to-text). Even for concepts that are highly unique to one modality (e.g. formal vs. colloquial language), steering vectors often induce a consistent, interpretable effect in the other modality, such as formal clothing and design. This transfer has a geometric signature too: despite a clear modality gap separating text and image representations, steering vectors with strong cross-modal transferability tend to point in similar directions for the same concept. Our findings shed light on how vision and language interact inside unified multimodal models and point towards more general, modality-agnostic approaches for controlling their behavior.|[2610.36269](http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36269)|
|**2026-10-28**|**Training-Free Inference Acceleration for Video Large Language Models: Methods, Trade-offs, and Evaluation**|Yuqi Li et.al.|Video Large Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in video understanding and reasoning, but processing long visual sequences incurs substantial computational, latency, and memory overhead. This survey examines training-free inference acceleration, focusing on reducing inference costs while preserving task-relevant spatiotemporal evidence. We organize existing methods by their intervention stages in the inference pipeline, covering input, visual encoding, projector, prefill, and decoding. Post-training quantization (PTQ) is discussed separately as a cross-stage extension with varying calibration requirements. We analyze how intervention position affects evidence preservation and computational savings, and why local efficiency improvements may not translate into end-to-end acceleration. We complement this analysis with quantitative evidence from prior studies and our own experiments under a shared evaluation setting to assess accuracy-latency trade-offs.|[2610.36327](http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36327)|
|**2026-10-28**|**CRLoMTL: Conflict-Resolution through Low-rank matrices for Multi-Task Learning**|Ahmed Agiza et.al.|Multi-task learning (MTL) improves model efficiency by sharing representations across related vision tasks, but it often suffers from negative transfer when task updates interfere with one another. Existing conflict-mitigation methods typically operate in gradient space, requiring explicit task-gradient manipulation and additional optimization steps. We propose Conflict-Resolution through Low-Rank Matrices for Multi-Task Learning (CRLoMTL), a parameter-efficient framework that mitigates task interference in the low-rank parameter-update space. CRLoMTL learns task-specific LoRA updates through task-specific passes, where each task updates its own low-rank matrices, and integrates these updates through global shared-subspace fusion. Specifically, we introduce a shared-subspace resolver based on singular value decomposition (SVD), referred to as the SVD resolver, which extracts a common low-dimensional orthonormal basis across task adapters and projects task updates into this shared space before merging them into a single deployment-time update. The resulting update can be folded into the backbone, preserving the inference structure of the original model without additional runtime branches. Experiments with Swin Transformer backbones on PASCAL-Context, NYUD-v2, and CelebA show that CRLoMTL achieves a favorable accuracy-parameter trade-off, improving over single-task baselines by up to 2.77% on PASCAL-Context, 5.03% on NYUD-v2, and 3.50% on CelebA, while training only a small fraction of the parameters used by single-task models.|[2610.36337](http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36337)|
|**2026-10-28**|**CrowdCC: Jointly Benchmarking Corruption Robustness and Deployment Quantization in Crowd Counting**|S Mahmudul Hasan et.al.|Crowd-counting models deployed on edge devices face two shifts: inputs are degraded along the capture and transmission pipeline, while models are quantized to satisfy resource constraints. Yet corruption robustness and deployment quantization are typically evaluated separately. We introduce CrowdCC, a controlled corruption benchmark that jointly evaluates these effects using 23 deployment-motivated corruptions at three severity levels, four crowd-counting datasets, and 26 models using A100 TensorRT engines at FP32, FP16, and post-training INT8 precision, paired with throughput and energy measurements from corresponding Jetson Orin NX configurations. The corruptions span six families, with head annotations adjusted when geometry or visibility changes. Our evaluation shows that capture-chain corruptions consistently produce the largest degradation across the evaluated models, while crowd density affects absolute and relative error differently. Clean accuracy does not fully predict corrupted performance. INT8 alters corruption robustness substantially more than FP16, with no systematic direction, and does not consistently improve latency or energy. INT8 inference efficiency is strongly associated with reformat overhead in the compiled engine, while slowdowns are also observed under limited INT8 coverage. Precision changes corrupted-error rankings and robustness-cost frontiers, showing why model selection must consider corruption robustness and measured deployment cost together. The code is available at https://github.com/Tulane-Computer-Architecture-Systems/CrowdCC-Release.|[2610.36340](http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36340)|
|**2026-10-28**|**BoxWorld: Let World Engines Control and Video Generators Render**|Zike Wu et.al.|We tackle the challenge of building real-time interactive video worlds with user-defined behaviors. Such worlds must track object states, apply interaction rules, and render the resulting consequences as users act. Yet existing end-to-end video world models typically learn interaction dynamics within the generator, making it difficult to specify object-level rules and reason about their consequences. In this work, we introduce BoxWorld, which separates interaction reasoning from generative rendering. Given user-specified rules, a coding agent creates a Box World Engine that determines interaction outcomes and exposes the resulting object states through a lightweight interface of layout boxes, persistent object attributes, and dynamic status variables, leaving appearance and physical effects to generative rendering. A Box-State Generative Renderer then renders this evolving state stream into video autoregressively, enabling online control over object motion, state switches, and conditional events. Rendering this state stream is non-trivial: the renderer must respond to object-level state updates in real time while remaining coherent with the generated history. To this end, we introduce a three-stage training strategy that learns object grounding from open-domain videos and state transitions from gameplay videos, both annotated automatically, and finally performs rollout distillation on self-generated histories. We further propose PairedStateBench, a paired benchmark for fine-grained interaction control. BoxWorld substantially outperforms end-to-end world models and remains competitive across multiple public benchmarks. Project page: https://boxworld-web.github.io.|[2610.36371](http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36371)|
|**2026-10-28**|**Evaluating Federated Vision-Language and Vision-Only Models for Privacy-Aware Breast Cancer Imaging**|Malithi Mithsara Wanniarachchi Kankanamge et.al.|Artificial intelligence (AI) shows promise for breast imaging, but limited labeled data, institutional data fragmentation, and privacy concerns hinder centralized training. We investigate a privacy-aware federated learning framework combining pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) with client-level differential privacy. We compare general-purpose CLIP models, biomedical BiomedCLIP, and an ImageNet-pretrained ViT-B/16 baseline on two public breast imaging datasets, with and without differential privacy. We also evaluate a CLIP ViT-B/16 ablation that removes the text pathway. Evaluation includes patient-level ROC-AUC with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals, baseline comparisons, threshold sensitivity, inter-model agreement, and communication cost. Under federated learning, all five models achieve high normal-versus-sick discrimination (ROC-AUC: 0.940-0.990). However, acquisition year alone achieves 0.974 on the same test partition, raising concerns about confounding rather than genuine pathology recognition. Benign-versus-malignant discrimination remains uncertain (ROC-AUC: 0.504-0.637), with all confidence intervals including 0.50. Removing the text pathway preserves classification accuracy while halving communication cost. Differential privacy reduces ROC-AUC by 0.375, attributable to perturbing the full model state rather than only trainable parameters. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating confounding, predictive reliability, privacy implementation, and deployment efficiency when developing federated AI systems for breast imaging.|[2610.36379](http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36379)|
|**2026-10-28**|**SOMA: A Benchmark for Fine-Grained Egocentric Behavior and Body-Motion Understanding**|Matea Tashkovska et.al.|Perceiving human body motion is critical for multimodal systems that understand and assist people. Yet current evaluations of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) largely focus on objects, scenes, and coarse actions, leaving their ability to reason about the body itself poorly assessed. This is especially challenging from the egocentric perspective, in which the body is only partially visible and motion must be inferred from occluded and temporally distributed cues. We introduce SOMA, a benchmark for fine-grained body-motion understanding from egocentric video, comprising 1,632 human-verified questions across three capability axes: body configuration, motion dynamics, and temporal reasoning. We evaluate 37 leading closed-source, open-source, and specialized egocentric MLLMs, complemented by an extensive human evaluation. We find that humans also find this task difficult from video alone (68.5% accuracy), yet clearly outperform the strongest MLLM (Qwen3.6-27B), which reaches 50.0% zero-shot accuracy. Our error analysis shows that MLLMs often misread the wearer's own body, misjudge events in time, and are prone to biases such as favoring the right hand or under-counting repetitions. To narrow the gap to human performance and support further progress, we introduce a training dataset of aligned video, body motion, and language supervision, and a multimodal baseline that jointly learns from these modalities. By identifying common failure modes and missing capabilities in current MLLMs, we hope SOMA will inspire future research on body-motion understanding and multimodal reasoning. Full benchmark, training data, and code will be released at: https://cnai.epfl.ch/soma|[2610.36384](http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36384)|
|**2026-10-28**|**ORBITAL: Optimization of Robust Brain--Computer Inference Through Architecture-Aware Low-Precision Compression**|Saim Rehman et.al.|Compact electroencephalography (EEG) decoders enable embedded brain--computer interfaces (BCIs), but compression can alter adversarial robustness without proportional hardware savings. We present ORBITAL, a robustness-constrained framework combining hardware-realizable structured compression, recovery-aware operating-point selection, multi-attack evaluation, and native edge validation. Across nine subjects and three seeds on BCI Competition IV-2a, S25-TRADES achieves the highest observed mean true-union robustness among compressed EEGNet models (23.06% vs 21.27% for standard Full), with 26.27% fewer parameters and 25.10% fewer MACs. Matched controls identify TRADES as the main source of robustness recovery, improving S25 union accuracy by 6.74 percentage points over clean recovery (p=0.0039), while per-example analysis reveals boundary redistribution rather than uniform margin expansion. On Jetson Orin Nano, FP16 compression reduces board energy by up to 16.20% and latency by 8.00%. Despite 99.3% prediction agreement, native INT8 Q/DQ incurs about twice the FP16 latency and energy, demonstrating the need for joint robustness and hardware-aware optimization.|[2610.36411](http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36411)|
|**2026-10-28**|**SpeeDiff: Scalable Pixel-Anchored End-to-End Latent Diffusion Model**|Bingliang Zhang et.al.|We present Scalable Pixel-anchored End-to-end Diffusion (SpeeDiff), a latent diffusion method that jointly trains the VAE and the diffusion model from scratch. In principle, joint training allows the diffusion loss gradient to directly guide the VAE encoder, encouraging the formation of a generation-friendly latent space and potentially yielding faster convergence than the conventional two-stage approach with a pretrained frozen VAE. However, a naive end-to-end implementation severely degrades performance, as unrestricted backpropagation of the diffusion loss leads to latent space collapse. Our main technical contribution is a simple yet effective Tweedie Pixel Reconstruction (TPR) loss, which provides additional pixel-level feedback by decoding a predicted clean latent from an intermediate noisy state using Tweedie's formula, thereby alleviating collapse. Furthermore, our method enables jointly scaling a fully transformer-based architecture and enhances representation alignment within the end-to-end framework. Our SpeeDiff-XL model achieves over 140x and 61x faster training compared to Vanilla SiT and REPA, respectively, while attaining an FID of 1.50 without guidance on ImageNet 256x256 generation. With a more efficient 32x compressed VAE, our model further reaches an FID of 1.53 without guidance on ImageNet 512x512 generation.|[2610.36419](http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36419)|
|**2026-10-28**|**SO-101 Bench: Accessible Spatial Manipulation**|Truman Hickok et.al.|Low-cost arms such as the SO-101 have become the most common entry point to robot learning, yet no released policy performs spatially constrained, language-conditioned tasks on them out of the box, and existing SO-101 benchmarks run only on physical hardware with simple tasks and few held-out objects. We introduce SO-101 Bench, a simulated benchmark for language-conditioned spatial manipulation built on an Isaac Lab digital twin of a real SO-101 setup. It has four tasks scored as five families, 138 objects in seen, unseen-instance and unseen-class splits, 916 evaluation episodes with subsets for held-out appearances, rotate-to-fit planning and occlusion memory, and 3,629 simulated demonstrations on which every learned policy is fine-tuned under an equal compute budget. The twin ranks policies as the real robot does: five policies trained without real data, four VLAs and an LLM agent, keep their exact ranking when the same weights run on the physical arm in an unseen environment with unseen objects (Spearman rho = 1.00, MMRV = 0.000), although simulation overestimates success. Across nine VLAs and world-action models, the best learned policies score near 61%, with spatial placement, unseen object classes and rotate-to-fit planning remaining open. An LLM agent that writes code and hands grasping to a learned policy scores 83.2%, and an ablation shows that this lead comes from the choice of harness and the choice of language model.|[2610.36420](http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36420)|
|**2026-10-28**|**FORESEE-MS: Toward Prospective Spatial Forecasting of Future Multiple Sclerosis Lesions from Baseline FLAIR MRI**|Maryam Akhavan Aghdam et.al.|Traditional multiple sclerosis (MS) image analysis has primarily focused on retrospectively detecting and segmenting lesions. This study investigates whether baseline FLAIR MRI can identify regions at risk for future lesion formation beyond population-level spatial patterns. We introduce FORESEE-MS, an evaluation protocol that uses a fold-specific population-prior atlas as a baseline and assesses predictions using pooled voxel-level discrimination (AUROC and AUPRC) and within-patient lesion localization (Recall@Top-K%), with patient-level bootstrap confidence intervals. We evaluated five deep learning models (3D U-Net, Attn+ResBlock+VAE, ViT, and two SwinUNETR variants) using 5-fold cross-validation on 39 subjects from the MSSEG-2 dataset. The atlas achieved the highest pooled voxel-level AUROC and AUPRC, with no deep learning model reliably outperforming it on either metric. However, the 3D U-Net and Attn+ResBlock+VAE achieved higher mean voxel-level within-patient Recall@Top-K% than the atlas at all evaluated thresholds, although most paired confidence intervals for the differences included zero. These findings suggest that baseline FLAIR may contain patient-specific predictive information, but in this small cohort, it remains uncertain whether this information improves lesion forecasting beyond a population-prior atlas.|[2610.36428](http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36428)|
|**2026-10-28**|**LociArt: A Unified Paradigm for Free-Style Local Video Stylization**|Yuxuan Chen et.al.|Video stylization typically transforms entire scenes, while local artistic editing requires precise region--style association, spatial control, and temporal consistency. We introduce LociArt, a unified paradigm for free-style local video stylization that explicitly specifies where to stylize and what style to apply while preserving non-target content. At its core, GRNStyle builds on Generative Refinement Networks (GRN) and introduces a polar style-aware mask that embeds style identities as equal-norm directions within selected regions. Complementary representation--geometry conditioning combines encoded mask features with raw-mask spatial support, integrating spatiotemporal context with geometric control. To provide paired supervision, we develop an automated pipeline combining global stylization, video object removal, matting, and compositing, and construct the LociArt-100K Dataset with 100K local stylization pairs. We further establish the LociArt Benchmark, comprising 80 source videos and 84 target masks covering 168 foreground/background stylization cases, with a Style Prototype Similarity (SPS) evaluation scheme for regional style quality and complementary measures of non-target preservation and temporal consistency. Experiments show that GRNStyle outperforms existing methods in regional style quality and spatial control while maintaining strong temporal consistency. Qualitative examples further illustrate joint stylization of multiple regions with the same or different learned styles, despite training only on single-region, single-style pairs. Together, these components provide a unified foundation for learning and evaluating controllable local video stylization. |**2026-10-28**|**Full Collapse Is Suboptimal: Controlled Partial Neural Collapse for Long-Tailed Recognition**|Hyeontaek Hwang et.al.|Recent long-tailed recognition (LTR) methods incorporate neural collapse (NC) and align features to a fixed Equiangular Tight Frame (ETF) as a uniform target for all classes. |**2026-10-28**|**ClusterSplat: Semantic Cluster Selection for 3D Visual Grounding in Gaussian Splatting**|Jaesung Lee et.al.|We study 3D visual grounding in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), where a referring expression should identify a target object as both a rendered 2D mask and a set of explicit 3D Gaussians. |**2026-10-28**|**Confident First, Reflective Second: Reinforcement Learning of Confidence-Preserving Reflection for Video Understanding**|Zihao Lin et.al.|Video models answer from sampled frames and may miss the decisive moment. |**2026-10-28**|**Spatial-Frequency Learning for Scanning Transmission Electron Microscopy Image Enhancement**|Hesong Li et.al.|Scanning Transmission Electron Microscopy (STEM) enables the observation of atomic arrangements at sub-angstrom resolution and plays a key role in the discovery and characterization of advanced materials. |**2026-10-28**|**GarmentSegAgent: Autonomous Garment Segmentation for Web Fashion Images via Textual Self-Refinement**|Jia Chen et.al.|Web fashion images support applications such as visual product search and consumer-to-shop matching, yet their visual heterogeneity makes reliable garment segmentation challenging. |**2026-10-28**|**ARISE: Authentic Reference-Informed Stability Enhancement for Continual Multimodal Forgery Detection**|Yuchen Zhang et.al.|Multimodal forgery detection is commonly studied under a static assumption: training attacks are expected to approximate those encountered after deployment. |**2026-10-28**|**Identity or Evidence? Auditing Evidence Dependence in Agentic Life-Science Benchmarks**|Danai Brilli et.al.|Agentic life-science benchmarks give an agent evidence about a named entity and score an answer against a recorded outcome. We examine this distinction by varying identity and evidence independently on a clinical-outcome benchmark and published tasks from Biomni and LAB-Bench. Blinding identity matters little when a prompt contains a decisive sequence or passage. It matters a great deal when the prompt is mostly a name and candidate list (0.742 named versus 0.082 blinded; chance 0.093). |**2026-10-28**|**Frugal Handwritten Text Recognition for Sub-Saharan Civil-Status Registers: A Smartphone-to-Records Pipeline with CPU-Only Inference**|Ousmane Hamadou et.al.|Handwritten civil-status registers across Sub-Saharan Africa are being photographed, but rarely transcribed, which leaves their content unsearchable. |**2026-10-28**|**FrameForge: Harnessing Priors of Video Foundation Models for Unified Image Generation**|Yijing Lin et.al.|Unified conditional image generation requires a single model to preserve different aspects of a visual input while producing a target image that follows textual guidance. |**2026-10-28**|**PRISM-BENCH: Diagnosing Grounded and Faithful Multimodal Reasoning Beyond Final-Answer Accuracy**|Vansh Bhatia et.al.|Final-answer accuracy reports whether a vision-language model was right, but not whether its answer was grounded in the image, whether its stated reasoning reflects that evidence, or what the answer cost to produce. |**2026-10-28**|**Decoupling Consistency and Conflict across MLLM Layers for Fake News Detection**|Kai Qian et.al.|The trustworthiness of Web content faces a growing threat from multimodal fake news. |**2026-10-28**|**LabWorld: Learning Interactive 4D Worlds for Scientific Experimentation**|Suozhi Huang et.al.|Autonomous scientific agents must not only reason about experiments but also interact with the physical environments in which they are executed. |**2026-10-28**|**WithinVAE: Compact Visual Autoencoding with Self-Distilled Semantics**|Yuzhou Ji et.al.|Visual autoencoders must balance reconstruction fidelity, compactness, and semantic structure. |**2026-10-28**|**4D Reconstruction with Events & RGB**|Dulanga Weerakoon et.al.|Reconstructing dynamic 3D scenes over time (4D reconstruction) from a single moving camera is central to robotics and AR/VR applications, yet state-of the-art feed-forward methods rely solely on RGB frames and therefore inherit the failure modes of conventional cameras, including motion blur and temporal aliasing under fast or non-uniform camera and object motion. |**2026-10-28**|**Adapting Video Models for Robot Control via Motion-guided Asymmetric Prediction**|Taeyoung Kim et.al.|World Action Models (WAMs) leverage pretrained video generative models for robotic control by jointly predicting future visual observations and actions. |**2026-10-28**|**SAGE: Semantic-Augmented Geometric Experts for Point Cloud Registration**|Tomoyasu Shimada et.al.|Point cloud registration is an essential task for scene reconstruction, requiring the alignment of partially overlapping point clouds. |**2026-10-28**|**Haste Makes Waste? Towards Safe Few-Step Text-to-Image Models**|Lior Ziv et.al.|While few-step distilled text-to-image models have gained traction due to their fast generation times, the speed-up implications on their unsafe generation rates remain unknown. |**2026-10-28**|**Look Only When Needed: Certificate-Guided Visual Routing for Efficient Diffusion VLMs**|Donghyeon Cho et.al.|Diffusion vision-language models (DVLMs) process their entire input at every denoising step. |**2026-10-28**|**SAGE: Saliency-Annealed Gated Encoder for Universal Vision Recognition**|Le Yang et.al.|When adapting self-supervised Vision Transformers (ViTs) to dense prediction, existing methods often treat the ViT as a passive feature extractor and may underuse the rich priors encoded in its representations, including saliency, global context, and high-frequency details. |**2026-10-28**|**Progressively Refining SAM for Accurate Phytoplankton Segmentation**|Jialin Li et.al.|Accurate phytoplankton segmentation is essential for ecological monitoring, yet it remains largely underexplored due to the subtle visual characteristics of phytoplankton and the scarcity of pixel-level annotations. |**2026-10-28**|**Hy-Nomas: Towards Free-form Interactive World Generation**|Qiaoling Chen et.al.|Interactive world generation requires models to follow successive commands while preserving relevant history and action consequences. |**2026-10-28**|**Readout and Operating-Point Sensitivity in Event-Stream Candidate Selection**|Yifan Shuai et.al.|Event-triggered recording needs a useful combination of target capture and false triggers, yet representation comparisons can change with readout and threshold calibration. |**2026-10-28**|**Systematic Morphometric Brain Autoencoding for Representation Learning in Neurodegenerative Diseases**|Nuria Balb\'as-Esteban et.al.|Early identification of neurodegenerative disorders using structural T1-weighted MRI is essential for timely clinical intervention, yet supervised deep learning models often struggle to generalize due to limited annotations and scanner-induced distribution shift. |**2026-10-28**|**GroundControl: Satellite-Conditioned Multi-View Diffusion for Reconstruction-Free Novel View Synthesis**|Akshay Krishnan et.al.|Multi-view or video diffusion models have recently emerged as state-of-the-art approaches for novel-view synthesis from sparse image collections. |**2026-10-28**|**ReferStream: Interactive Subject Injection for Streaming Video Generation**|Shuolin Xu et.al.|Injecting new subjects naturally during streaming video generation requires integrating newly supplied visual references into the existing video while preserving established subjects and the scene. Project page: https://xushuolin.github.io/ReferStream/.|[2610.37566](http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37566)|
|**2026-10-28**|**The Noise Plane: A Diffusion Bridge Across Exponent and Dispersion**|Xuran Hu et.al.|Diffusion-based denoising commonly uses Gaussian perturbations, whereas sensor noise follows diverse signal-dependent statistical laws. |**2026-10-28**|**As the Story Unfolds: Watching a Film and Identifying Characters as a Human Does**|Zhongrui Gui et.al.|Films introduce characters incrementally as they progress. |**2026-10-28**|**Zero-Shot Multimodal Event Spotting in Soccer Broadcasts**|Sadia Kamal et.al.|Automatic soccer event spotting supports highlight generation, video indexing, and sports analytics, but existing methods depend on large annotated datasets and soccer-specific training. |**2026-10-28**|**MoI-Bench: A Benchmark for Image Generation and Editing on Mobile Devices**|Kailai Feng et.al.|Developing on-device image models requires considering practical user needs, task types and device resource constraints. |**2026-10-28**|**VideoLVR: Latent Visual Reasoning over Grounded Video Evidence**|Shilong Li et.al.|Chain-of-thought reasoning has substantially advanced video understanding in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). |**2026-10-28**|**Perceiving and Predicting Dynamic Sports: Spatiotemporal Intelligence in Vision Models for Egocentric Tennis Video**|Tudor Braicu et.al.|Agile robots require spatiotemporal intelligence to interpret scenes, reason about interactions, and anticipate future events. |**2026-10-28**|**Know, then Draw: A New Learning Paradigm for Visual Generation**|Yucheng Mao et.al.|Visual generation requires both high-level semantic knowledge and fine-grained pixel details. |**2026-10-28**|**Repurposing Video Diffusion Transformers for Cross-View Temporal Object Correspondence**|Siyoon Jin et.al.|Cross-view object correspondence identifies the same object across views. |**2026-10-28**|**Can Discrete Tokens Serve as Semantically Lossless Representations of Visual Signals?**|Jialv Zou et.al.|Discrete visual tokens represent vision in a discrete form analogous to language, offering a native interface for multimodal modeling under a shared next-token prediction objective. |**2026-10-28**|**Honeycomb-Surfels: Compact Hexagonal Primitives for Efficient Scene Rendering and Reconstruction**|Prakhar Kaushik et.al.|Novel view synthesis and 3D reconstruction have advanced rapidly with radiance fields and splatting, yet their memory and computational demands limit their use in resource-constrained settings. |**2026-10-28**|**Real-Time Smart Retail Analytics through Fog Computing using the RetailLightNet Lightweight Model**|Mayank Atreya et.al.|Smart retail systems now depend on the application of real-time video analytics, which can track customer behavior, manage shelf inventory, and enhance in-store processes. |**2026-10-28**|**From Slices to Volumes: Comparing 2D, 2.5D, and 3D Residual Networks for Pulmonary Nodule Malignancy-Risk Classification**|Bahodir Nazarov et.al.|Purpose: To compare 2D, 2.5D, and 3D residual networks for pulmonary nodule malignancy-risk classification and evaluate momentum-contrast pretraining, mild augmentation, and exclusion of indeterminate ratings. |**2026-10-28**|**Knowledge distillation across teacher architectures for compact diabetic retinopathy grading**|Mossa Manisa et.al.|Diabetic retinopathy grading from retinal fundus photographs is important but difficult to deploy on resource-constrained hardware. |**2026-10-28**|**OmniBrain-0: A Unified Agentic Model for Embodied Intelligence**|Xiaomi Embodied Intelligence Team et.al.|General-purpose embodied intelligence requires robots to coordinate diverse skills over long horizons, track task progress, and recover from failures. |**2026-10-28**|**The Trinity:Capability-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Multimodal Agents**|Weidong Tang et.al.|Multimodal intelligence can be viewed as human-guided co-evolution between worlds and agents through interaction. |**2026-10-28**|**Closed-Loop Aware Planning via Imitation-Free Speed Scoring for End-to-End Autonomous Driving**|Emad Aghajanzadeh et.al.|End-to-end autonomous driving has predominantly relied on open-loop imitation learning for training, which presents two limitations. |**2026-10-28**|**A Heart Means Recursion: Exploring Visual Meaning and Communication in VLMs**|Alexa R. Tartaglini et.al.|Do vision-language models (VLMs) share our ability to communicate visually? |**2026-10-28**|**PRISM: Pathology Reliability In Scarce-label Medicine. |**2026-10-28**|**Camera-to-Quadruped Robot Pose Estimation from Sequential Images**|Seobin Hwang et.al.|Quadruped robots are increasingly deployed in hazardous environments such as disaster response and facility inspection, where external-camera monitoring is essential for safe operation. |**2026-10-28**|**Image Modeling: From Handcrafted Priors to Foundation Image Models**|A. Murat Tekalp et.al.|This paper unifies six decades of image modeling, evolving from handcrafted mathematical tractable priors to solve inverse problems in imaging to data-driven deep foundation image models for both image generation and solving inverse problems, under a common Bayesian framework that formulates image modeling as an implicit or explicit probabilistic characterization of a data manifold. |**2026-10-28**|**TAPESTRY: A Single Backbone for Video Generation and Robot Control**|Jeremy A. |**2026-10-28**|**Tail Cues, Principal Corrections: Plug-and-Play Rectification for Open-Set Test-Time Adaptation**|Yingkai Yang et.al.|Open-Set Test-Time Adaptation (OSTTA) operates on non-stationary target streams where covariate and semantic shifts coexist. |**2026-10-28**|**GUI-JEPA: Candidate-Conditioned JEPA Latents as a Fast Action Policy for Mobile GUI Agents**|Bingchao Wang et.al.|Mobile GUI agents are typically fine-tuned 7B-scale vision-language models (VLMs) that generate each action as text. |**2026-10-28**|**Quantized Edge Inference of a Self-Supervised SAR-Optical Encoder on Commodity x86 Hardware**|Christian Sanchez-Leon et.al.|Self-supervised vision transformers are increasingly used as reusable encoders for Earth observation, but their inference cost on the hardware available in the field is rarely characterized. |**2026-10-28**|**Label-free cell counting and viability prediction with brightfield imaging and deep learning**|Amir Reza Vazifeh et.al.|Cell viability assessment is a core requirement in cell culture systems, with critical applications in biopharmaceutical manufacturing and drug development. |**2026-10-28**|**Counting the Bandages: On measuring the time that AI saves**|Solomon Shalom Lijo et.al.|I consider what it means for AI assistance to save time. The argument has four parts. I define a model-free pair of quantities, time saved and excess escaped defects, and one decision number built from them: the break-even defect cost. I give a baseline model of checking in which, until the model is good enough not to check, a calibrated worker's escaped-defect rate does not depend on how good the model is; checking time grows with the logarithm of the model's error rate; and over-trust buys minutes on the clock at a larger cost in total minutes. I show what randomized studies can and cannot identify, and I replicate METR's developer study from its public data: the same 246 issues support a slowdown of 19% or 24% depending on the estimand (34% without adjusting for a chance imbalance), and AI helped on somewhere between 3% and 82% of them. Finally, I restate the published record, with stated bounds in place of imported point assumptions. In GDPval's own review-every-output workflow, review time alone caps GPT-5's speedup at 3.6x; the consultants outside the frontier were faster, and more often wrong. Last, I test two of the model's predictions in a small pre-specified experiment on AI reviewers checking AI drafts of the same kind of brief, built from SEC filings made after the models' training data were collected. |**2026-10-28**|**I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop**|Samuel Breckenridge et.al.|Human oversight is a pillar of AI safety.
